title: Human Judgment in the Agent Workflow
stat: 69 percent of UX researchers now use AI in at least some of their projects, a 19-point jump from last year
source: A published industry survey of UX researchers this year
topic_claim: human judgment in agent workflows is the fixed line
story_examples: One agent scanned four hundred papers and chose the twelve that counted as sources.
Another ranked a season of interview notes by strategic fit against our scoring sheet.
A third drafted the synthesis report before anyone opened the raw quote file.
thesis: The question stops being human versus machine and becomes architecture: which judgment calls stay human, which get automated, and who verifies both. The machine's rationale needs to be on the record. Expose the calls, and the boundary moves by design
design_moves: log what got filtered before you looked
counter: Teams lean on the boundary when they configure their workflows. The framing reads as prudence, and prudence calms stakeholders more than it protects the research
definition: Judgment surface is the set of calls an agent workflow makes before a human reads a word
gap_stat_a: 61 percent of researchers trust AI to find patterns
gap_stat_b: only 47.6 percent trust it to turn patterns into recommendations
takeaway: Build for traceability: keep interpretation human, expose the rationale, log every filter.
question_tail: Where in your workflow does human judgment still make a call you never see?
person_context: I have spent the past year building AI-augmented research workflows
